verdict.rationale: One passage, John 13:1-17, carries nearly the whole weight, and its own vocabulary is genuinely two-edged. The obligation verb "you ought" (opheilete) in John 13:14 (lemma "to owe" (opheilo), lexically to owe, a debt or binding duty) plus the purpose clause "that as I did, you also should do" (hina kathos ego epoiesa kai hymeis poiete) in John 13:15 supply a real warrant for ongoing imitation, which the ordinance reading leans on. But the noun that frames it, "example" or "pattern" (hypodeigma) in John 13:15, is lexically a pattern, illustration, a picture showing how something is to be done, used elsewhere even for negative examples (Hebrews 4:11, 2 Peter 2:6), so it marks a model to be copied morally rather than a cultic rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual). The same chapter pivots from physical "wash" (niptein) to spiritual "clean" (katharos) in John 13:10-11, showing John reading the act as a sign. The words establish a binding pattern of reciprocal lowly service but do not by themselves rank the specific act as a third standing ordinance, so the verdict is recorded as disputed.

scripture.reasoning: The "if-then" clause beginning with "if then I washed your feet, the Lord and the Teacher" (ei oun ego enipsa hymon tous podas, ho kyrios kai ho didaskalos) draws the result "you also ought to wash one another's feet" (kai hymeis opheilete allelon niptein tous podas). The verb "you ought" (opheilete) is present-tense (an ongoing, simple statement of fact) and lexically means to owe, to be under binding obligation, and "one another" (allelon) makes the duty reciprocal among believers. The grammar establishes a binding pattern of mutual service. It does not itself specify whether the obligation is the literal washing repeated as a rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual) or the servant attitude it embodies, the same "to owe" (opheilo) plus "one another" (allelon) pairing that elsewhere in the Johannine corpus (the writings of John) governs the duty to love one another.

"For I have given you an example, that as I did, you also should do" (hypodeigma gar edoka hymin hina kathos ego epoiesa kai hymeis poiete). The noun "example" or "pattern" (hypodeigma) is lexically a sign, illustration, a picture showing how something is to be done, a pattern or specimen set before others. Across its other canonical uses it marks a model to be copied or, in Hebrews 4:11 and 2 Peter 2:6, a warning example to be avoided, never the installation of a cultic rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual). The purpose clause "so that" (hina) with the present subjunctive "you may do" (poiete) frames ongoing action, so the clause can ground either a literal ongoing washing or imitation of the self-lowering it displays.

"The one who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean" (ho leloumenos ouk echei chreian ei me tous podas nipsasthai, all estin katharos holos), then "and you are clean" (kai hymeis katharoi este). Jesus contrasts the bathed person (perfect passive participle, a completed past action with continuing effect in the passive form, of "to bathe" (louo)) who needs only the feet washed with being wholly clean, then applies "clean" (katharos) to the disciples spiritually. The pivot from physical "to wash" (niptein) to spiritual "clean" (katharos) shows John reading the act as a sign that points beyond itself, which complicates treating the foot-washing primarily as a standing ritual ordinance.

"If she has washed the saints' feet" (ei hagion podas enipsen) lists washing the saints' feet among the good works ("good works", ergois kalois) qualifying a widow for support, alongside raising children, showing hospitality, and relieving the afflicted. The act appears as one item in a catalogue of private charitable deeds, not as a churchwide rite ranked with baptism and the table, which weighs against treating it as a third standing ordinance. The same verb "to wash" (nipto) here describes ordinary domestic washing, the dominant sense of the word across the canon.

"If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them" (ei tauta oidate, makarioi este ean poiete auta). The beatitude (a blessing-statement) attaches blessing to doing these things, "if" (ean) with the present subjunctive of ongoing action, which a reading favoring a perpetual ordinance leans on, since the blessing is conditioned on continued practice rather than on a single past observance. The plural pronouns "these things" (tauta) and "them" (auta) take as their nearest antecedent the whole lesson of humble service in John 13:12-16, so the conditioned blessing can fall on the servant disposition generally rather than on a discrete repeated rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual).

complicating_texts.resolution: "You ought to wash one another's feet" (opheilete allelon niptein) is the strongest pro-ordinance datum because "to owe" (opheilo) states a binding obligation, lexically a debt, in present-tense (ongoing, simple statement of fact) terms. It is addressed by noting the immediate ground is "I washed yours" (ego enipsa hymon), the Lord washing servants, so the obligation reverses status rather than installing a liturgy (a fixed order of worship), and the reciprocal "one another" (allelon) parallels the Johannine duty (the duty taught in John's writings) to love one another (1 John 3:16, 1 John 4:11) where the same obligation verb governs an ethic, not a rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual). The grammar supports a binding duty but does not disambiguate (does not settle the choice between) literal repetition from imitation of the posture, leaving the ordinance question open on the words alone.

"Example" (hypodeigma) plus "so that you may do" (hina poiete) is resolved by the lexical range of "example" (hypodeigma), which denotes a sign, illustration, a picture showing how something is to be done, a model held up for imitation, used elsewhere even of negative warning examples. A specimen-to-copy sense fits both a perpetual literal washing and imitation of self-abasement (self-lowering), so it confirms ongoing imitation is commanded but does not by itself elevate the specific act to a rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual) ranked with baptism and the Supper. The OpenBible cross-reference weight on this verse points to imitation-of-Christ texts (imitatio texts) (1 Peter 2:21, 1 John 2:6) rather than rite-institution texts.

The "blessed are you if you do them" (makarioi este ean poiete auta) beatitude (blessing-statement) conditions blessing on continued doing. It is addressed by observing that "these things" (tauta) and "them" (auta) have as their nearest antecedent the whole lesson of humble service introduced in John 13:12-16, so the blessing can fall on the servant disposition generally rather than on a discrete repeated rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual). The text therefore underdetermines (does not provide enough information to settle) the ordinance claim.

"She has washed the saints' feet" (podas enipsen) sits in a list of private charitable acts (raising children, hospitality, relieving the afflicted), which an ordinance reading would not predict, since a churchwide rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual) ranked with baptism would be expected to surface in instructions on assembly practice rather than in a widow-qualification catalogue. This weighs against ordinance status but is not decisive, since the same act could be both a personal kindness and a corporate practice in some settings.

A direct query of the lexical store returned zero VariantUnit nodes reading at John.13.x or 1 Timothy 5:10, and the bundle reports "not_in_ecm_scope" (outside the critical edition's scope) as true with an empty variant_units list. Known SBLGNT editorial sigla (editorial markings in the Society of Biblical Literature Greek New Testament) in John 13 (word-order notes in John 13:2, bracketing near "my hands" (mou tas cheiras) in John 13:9) do not bear on whether an ongoing ordinance is instituted, so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: "You ought" (opheilete) in John 13:14 is a genuine obligation-verb of duty (to owe, to be bound), reinforced by "I washed yours" (ego enipsa hymon) and the explicit "just as I did" (kathos ego epoiesa), and the conditional ("if-then" clause) beatitude (blessing-statement) in John 13:17 ties blessing to continued doing. On this reading "so that you also should do" (hina kai hymeis poiete) commands the act itself, and 1 Timothy 5:10 shows the early assemblies preserved literal foot-washing, so the words install a third standing practice alongside baptism and the Supper.

"Example" (hypodeigma) is lexically a pattern or illustration to be imitated (a picture showing how something is to be done), not a cultic-institution term (a term for founding a sacred ceremony), and is used even of negative examples; the symbolic pivot to "clean" (katharos) in John 13:10-11 spiritualizes the act; "to owe" (opheilo) plus "one another" (allelon) mirrors the Johannine duty (duty taught in John's writings) to love one another rather than a liturgy (fixed order of worship); and 1 Timothy 5:10 lists it among private charitable deeds. So the lexical pattern grounds an ethic of mutual lowly service rather than a rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual) ranked with baptism and the Supper.

hermeneutics.notes: Both lenses are defensible from the Greek alone. The decisive interpretive move is whether "example" (hypodeigma) and "you ought" (opheilete) govern the specific act of washing or the disposition it dramatizes, and the words do not force the choice. The principle of comparing Scripture with Scripture (analogia_scripturae) is engaged through 1 Timothy 5:10, the only other canonical mention of the act, and through the OpenBible cross-reference network on John 13:14-15, which points to servant-humility and imitation-of-Christ (imitatio-Christi) texts (Luke 22:26, Galatians 5:13, Philippians 2:2, 1 Peter 2:21, 1 Peter 5:5) rather than to baptism or Supper institution. That canonical weight tilts away from ordinance status without closing the question.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Does John 13:1-17 institute foot-washing as an ongoing ordinance of the Church, alongside baptism and the Lord's Supper, or does it set an exemplary pattern of servant love that the act dramatizes?
stem_audit.notes: The stem (the question as originally framed) asserts the act was not instituted as an ongoing ordinance and pre-labels it a beautiful pattern of servant love, which loads the conclusion of one reading into the question. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form keeps both the ordinance and the exemplary-service readings live so the lexical data can adjudicate (decide) rather than the framing. VERDICT-CHANGED: not applicable here, the verdict is unchanged from the prior evidence file: still disputed. Direct lexical-store queries confirmed and refined the counts ("to owe" (opheilo) 37 tokens, "example" (hypodeigma) 7 tokens across 6 verses, "to wash" (nipto) 17) and added real OpenBible cross-reference edges, but did not lexically force a flip away from disputed.

lay_summary: Everything here turns on one passage, John 13:1-17, plus a single supporting line in 1 Timothy 5:10. In the Greek of John 13:14 Jesus says "you ought" (opheilete) to wash one another's feet, and in John 13:15 he calls what he did an "example" or "pattern" (hypodeigma), adding a purpose clause so that you also should do as I have done. The verb "you ought" (opheilete) carries the idea of owing, a binding duty, and the words plainly command ongoing imitation. What they do not settle by themselves is whether the thing to be repeated is the literal act of washing feet, kept as a standing rite (a ceremony or sacred ritual) next to baptism and the Lord's table, or the lowly servant love that the washing acts out. The key noun points toward the second reading. "Example" (hypodeigma) means a pattern, an illustration, a picture showing how something is to be done, and elsewhere it can even name a warning example to avoid, so it describes a model to be copied rather than a ceremony to be installed. The same chapter pushes the same direction. In John 13:10 Jesus shifts from physical washing "to wash" (nipto) to being "clean" (katharos) in a spiritual sense, telling the disciples you are clean, which treats the foot-washing as a sign that points beyond itself. The only other place the act appears, 1 Timothy 5:10, lists washing the saints' feet among private good works that qualify a widow for support, beside raising children and showing hospitality, which reads like personal kindness rather than a churchwide ordinance. The wider web of related verses linked to John 13:14-15 also points to humility and serving one another, not to rite-founding texts. So the evidence genuinely cuts both ways. The command to keep doing it is clear, but whether what must continue is the specific rite or the humility it embodies is not decided by the words alone. For that reason the finding is recorded as disputed, with the words leaning against ranking the act as a third standing ordinance but not ruling out continued literal practice.
